The apostolic Church

History and saints · Church history

The apostolic Church

4 sectionsNot completed
Notes

St. Ignatius and St. Irenaeus describe connections between apostolic teaching, bishops and the Eucharistic life of the Church. Apostolic succession means continuity of ministry from the apostles through those entrusted with care of the churches.[1][2]

How does St. Ignatius connect the bishop and the Eucharist?[1]

St. Ignatius describes the Eucharist as celebrated by the bishop or someone authorized by him. He relates the community’s visible unity to the bishop’s ministry and names priests and deacons alongside him. The passage is his particular account of ordered church life and sacramental oversight.[1]

Read original passage

Ignatius: the bishop and the Eucharist

See that ye all follow the bishop, even as Jesus Christ does the Father, and the presbytery as ye would the apostles; and reverence the deacons, as being the institution of God. Let no man do anything connected with the Church without the bishop. Let that be deemed a proper Eucharist, which is [administered] either by the bishop, or by one to whom he has entrusted it. Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude [of the people] also be; even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church. It is not lawful without the bishop either to baptize or to celebrate a love-feast; but whatsoever he shall approve of, that is also pleasing to God, so that everything that is done may be secure and valid.

Why does St. Irenaeus appeal to succession?[2]

St. Irenaeus presents apostolic teaching as publicly identifiable through the churches and the bishops entrusted with them. He contrasts that account with claims to a hidden teaching reserved for an elite. The passage connects succession with the faithful discharge of responsibility, rather than merely the possession of a title.[2]

Read original passage

Irenaeus: apostolic succession

It is within the power of all, therefore, in every Church, who may wish to see the truth, to contemplate clearly the tradition of the apostles manifested throughout the whole world; and we are in a position to reckon up those who were by the apostles instituted bishops in the Churches, and [to demonstrate] the succession of these men to our own times; those who neither taught nor knew of anything like what these [heretics] rave about. For if the apostles had known hidden mysteries, which they were in the habit of imparting to “the perfect” apart and privily from the rest, they would have delivered them especially to those to whom they were also committing the Churches themselves. For they were desirous that these men should be very perfect and blameless in all things, whom also they were leaving behind as their successors, delivering up their own place of government to these men; which men, if they discharged their functions honestly, would be a great boon [to the Church], but if they should fall away, the direst calamity.

St. Ignatius’ letter in its published collection[1]

The linked page supplies the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans in a historical collection that identifies its versions. It provides the surrounding source for the excerpt concerning bishop, community and Eucharist.[1]
